File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or SHA1 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or MD5 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or SHA1 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or MD5 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit updater spawning script/LOLBin or writing PE to user-writable path (supply-chain)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER known-bad SHA1 hash on file write or process execution · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 callback to known infrastructure (IPs + domains) · [LLM] Sustained low-rate beaconing from single host to OceanLotus C2 IP set (long-tail intrusion signal) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 callback to known infrastructure (IPs + domains) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound network connections or DNS resolutions to the specific C2 IPs and domains used by OceanLotus's SPECTRALVIPER backdoor across both the FireAnt Metakit supply-chain campaign and the 18-month construction-firm intrusion (mid-2024 - Feb 2026). Rationale: Uses the article's full C2 IOC table (Table 2 + IP/domain list) for the SPECTRALVIPER infrastructure. Both the early-2024-2026 construction-firm intrusion and the FireAnt supply-chain campaign reused subsets of this infrastructure, so any hit is article-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform / sandbox detonation lab that intentionally calls out to the same C2 IOCs for validation
  • Security researcher pivot/curl from a corporate analyst workstation
  • Stale Recorded Future/AlienVault enrichment job hitting these as 'check liveness' probes
  • DNS resolver cache poisoning resulting in legitimate domains briefly resolving to these IPs (very rare)
  • Honeypot or canary host deliberately deployed to attract OceanLotus traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msftsbox.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Cisco\"
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: pull all DeviceProcessEvents on the source host for ±10 min around the hit; identify the InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath driving the connection and SHA1/SHA256 of that binary. Cross-check the hash against UC2 hash list and against the OS vendor. Step 2 - Contain: isolate the device in Defender, block the matched IP/domain at the proxy/EDR network-blocklist, suspend the user's AAD session, and snapshot RAM if forensics capacity exists - SPECTRALVIPER is memory-resident. Step 3 - Hunt: pivot on the parent process and any sibling processes; sweep the enterprise for the same SHA1/SHA256 and for connections to the entire OceanLotus IP/domain set in the last 90d; check FireAnt Metakit installs across the fleet.
let OceanLotusIPs = dynamic(["139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);
let OceanLotusDomains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
union
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteIP in (OceanLotusIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (OceanLotusDomains)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Source="DeviceNetworkEvents"
),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | extend Q = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).query)
  | where Q has_any (OceanLotusDomains) or RemoteUrl has_any (OceanLotusDomains)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl=coalesce(RemoteUrl,Q), RemotePort, Source="DnsQueryResponse"
)
| order by Timestamp desc

let OceanLotusDomains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);

  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Source="CommonSecurityLog"
),

SPECTRALVIPER known-bad SHA1 hash on file write or process execution AIInstallation High
Alerts on any file written or process executed whose SHA1 matches one of the 20 SPECTRALVIPER / OceanLotus loader/payload hashes published in the ESET report. Covers both the construction-firm campaign and the FireAnt Metakit supply-chain. Rationale: Pure hash IOC match against the 20 SHA1 values published in the ESET article. These are tied to confirmed SPECTRALVIPER samples (both old/reused and the heavily-obfuscated stable build per Table 1) - any hit on managed endpoints is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/software/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR test lab intentionally executing the public SPECTRALVIPER samples for tuning
  • Threat-hunter who downloaded the samples from VT/MalwareBazaar onto a sandbox workstation
  • Incident-response forensic image being mounted/scanned on an analyst host
  • Sample triage by malware research team in a contained VLAN
  • Re-detection of the same artefact after a previous remediation that didn't purge backups
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox-01","malware-vm","ir-workstation") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Users\malware-analyst\"
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned malware-analysis sandbox; pull the InitiatingProcessFileName and full ancestry; check whether the binary lives in %ProgramData%, %AppData%, %Temp%, or a FireAnt Metakit install dir (article-specific delivery vectors). Step 2 - Contain: isolate the device, force-quarantine the file via Defender, revoke any tokens/sessions for the AccountName, and snapshot memory before reboot - SPECTRALVIPER has orchestration capabilities and may have injected. Step 3 - Hunt: pivot to the C2 IOCs in UC1 from this host over the last 90d; enumerate every other endpoint with the same SHA1 in DeviceFileEvents (including non-executed file landings); check ASEPs / scheduled tasks / services created by the InitiatingProcess.

FireAnt Metakit updater spawning script/LOLBin or writing PE to user-writable path (supply-chain) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the FireAnt Metakit Vietnamese stock-investment client (Oct 2025 - Mar 2026 supply-chain compromise) acting as parent to script hosts, LOLBins, or writing PE/DLL payloads to %AppData%/%ProgramData%/%Temp% - the behaviour observed when its compromised update server delivered SPECTRALVIPER. Rationale: Article names FireAnt Metakit as the compromised Vietnamese stock-investment platform whose update server delivered SPECTRALVIPER from Oct 2025 to Mar 2026 (Table 1: 2025-10-02 first iteration / 2025-10-17 stable). Pivots on the FireAnt parent process - which should never legitimately spawn script hosts or download tools - plus PE drops to user-writable dirs. Both branches are article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FireAnt auto-updater shelling out to PowerShell for post-install registration (low likelihood - most installers use msiexec)
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a FireAnt crash by attaching cmd.exe via process explorer
  • FireAnt installer running NSIS uninstall script that legitimately calls cmd.exe
  • Endpoint security agent injecting a hook into FireAnt processes that appears as a child
  • Repackaged-by-IT MSI deployment running custom install scripts under a FireAnt context
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-RegisterPackage" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--silent-install"
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: capture the FireAnt installation path + version, the child cmd-line in full, and SHA1 of both parent and child binaries; check whether the parent SHA1 matches UC2 list. Inventory FireAnt deployment fleet-wide via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory. Step 2 - Contain: isolate the host, block FireAnt update-server FQDNs at the proxy until vendor confirms a clean build, freeze the user's brokerage/email sessions (stock-investor context = high-value target per article). Step 3 - Hunt: sweep all FireAnt hosts in the org for connections to the UC1 C2 IOCs over the same time window; check if FireAnt update files dropped on disk have non-vendor signatures or differ in size/hash from a known-good golden image; pivot to AccountName for any Vietnamese-domain user activity related to securities/financial-regulator topics.
let FireAntParents = dynamic(["fireant.exe","fireantmetakit.exe","metakit.exe","fireant_updater.exe","fireantupdater.exe"]);
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msiexec.exe"]);
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (FireAntParents) or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
  | where FileName in~ (SuspChildren)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA1, Pivot="FireAnt_child_lolbin"
),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (FireAntParents) or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
  | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
  | where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".scr" or FileName endswith ".lnk"
  | where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\",@"\ProgramData\",@"\Temp\",@"\Public\")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, Pivot="FireAnt_drops_PE"
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let FireAntParents = dynamic(["fireant.exe","fireantmetakit.exe","metakit.exe","fireant_updater.exe","fireantupdater.exe"]);
let SuspChildren = dynamic([@"\powershell.exe",@"\pwsh.exe",@"\cmd.exe",@"\mshta.exe",@"\wscript.exe",@"\cscript.exe",@"\rundll32.exe",@"\regsvr32.exe",@"\bitsadmin.exe",@"\certutil.exe",@"\curl.exe",@"\wget.exe",@"\msiexec.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any (FireAntParents) or ParentProcessName has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
| where NewProcessName has_any (SuspChildren)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType, Pivot="FireAnt_child_lolbin"
| union ( ImFileEvent
         | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
         | where ActingProcessName has_any (FireAntParents) or ActingProcessName has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
         | where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","dll","scr","lnk")
         | where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\",@"\ProgramData\",@"\Temp\",@"\Public\")
         | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, ParentProcessName=ActingProcessName, NewProcessName=TargetFilePath, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, TokenElevationType="", Pivot="FireAnt_drops_PE" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sustained low-rate beaconing from single host to OceanLotus C2 IP set (long-tail intrusion signal) AICommand & Control Medium
Surfaces the 18-month construction-firm intrusion pattern (mid-2024 - Feb 2026): a single host with sustained, periodic, low-rate connections to one of the SPECTRALVIPER C2 IPs across many distinct hours and days. Tuned to catch the patient long-haul implant rather than a noisy beacon. Rationale: Article emphasises a 'prolonged espionage operation' (mid-2024 - Jan 2026, ~18 months) against a Vietnamese infrastructure & transport construction company - a low-rate sustained-presence shape. Statistical aggregation on the 8 published C2 IPs surfaces hosts with multi-day periodic contact, the long-tail signal the volumetric beaconing rules would miss. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running scheduled IOC-validation probes against the C2 IPs from a fixed scanning host
  • Threat-intel platform / Recorded Future / GreyNoise enrichment crawler hitting the same IPs
  • VPN concentrator or web proxy that aggregates all egress through one source IP (will look like sustained contact)
  • CDN/cloud-host customer who legitimately uses one of these IPs after OceanLotus moved off it (re-allocation)
  • Misconfigured SOC honeypot deployed at the perimeter
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("soc-scanner-01","tip-enrichment-01","recordedfuture-probe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","qualys.exe","masscan.exe","nmap.exe","zgrab.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: confirm the source IP/host is not a SOC scanner or TIP enrichment platform; pull all InitiatingProcessFileName / InitiatingProcessCommandLine + SHA1 for connections to the IP; check process ancestry for FireAnt Metakit (UC3) and SPECTRALVIPER hashes (UC2). Step 2 - Contain: network-isolate the device; collect memory + AutoRuns; revoke the AccountName's tokens; block all 8 OceanLotus C2 IPs at perimeter firewall regardless of this host. Step 3 - Hunt: extend the lookback to 18 months on this host and on any host sharing the same AccountName or same subnet; correlate to AAD signins from Vietnamese-IP geos; search file-share access logs for sensitive project / financial-regulator / Blazing Furnace investigation materials.
let OceanLotusIPs = dynamic(["139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (OceanLotusIPs)
| extend HourBucket = bin(Timestamp, 1h), DayBucket = startofday(Timestamp)
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctHours = dcount(HourBucket),
            DistinctDays = dcount(DayBucket),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 20),
            Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 20),
            CmdSamples = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 10)
            by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where DistinctDays >= 3 and DistinctHours >= 6
| extend CampaignSpanDays = datetime_diff('day', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| order by DistinctDays desc, CampaignSpanDays desc
let OceanLotusIPs = dynamic(["139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP in (OceanLotusIPs)
  | extend Src=SourceIP, Dst=DestinationIP, User=coalesce(SourceUserName,"")
),

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| sort - count

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query

| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"

    by src, second_level_domain

| sort - qcount

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    ( ImProcessCreate

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ShinyHunters CVE-2026-35273 exploit POST to PeopleSoft /PSEMHUB/hub · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] JSP webshell drop under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MeshCentral Azure-disguised agent + azurenetfiles.net C2 channel · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] WebLogic/Java spawning Linux recon shell after PSEMHUB exploit · [LLM] ShinyHunters fanout.sh SSH credential spray from PeopleSoft host · [LLM] zstd / pv archive staging of PeopleSoft exfil on application host · [LLM] ShinyHunters defacement README drop on PeopleSoft hosts
ShinyHunters CVE-2026-35273 exploit POST to PeopleSoft /PSEMHUB/hub AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POSTs to the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub endpoint (/PSEMHUB/hub) and the Integration Broker (/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector) — the two attack surfaces the ShinyHunters gadget chain abuses for unauthenticated RCE per CVE-2026-35273. Also flags any source matching the published staging IP range. Rationale: Targets the EXACT URI paths Mandiant/GTIG attribute to the CVE-2026-35273 gadget chain (/PSEMHUB/hub, /PSEMHUB/envmetadata, /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector) plus the published staging /29 (142.11.200.186-190) and the secondary attacker host 108.174.202.99. Defender query is downgraded to inbound-IP because DeviceNetworkEvents has no URI field. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/11/oracle-peoplesoft-under-attack-cve-2026-35273/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/shinyhunters-exploits-oracle-peoplesoft.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Oracle support engineer running EMHub diagnostics from an allowlisted bastion IP
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Qualys, Tenable, Rapid7) probing PSEMHUB endpoints as part of an authorised scan window
  • PeopleSoft Integration Broker server-to-server message traffic from a trusted partner SI to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector
  • Pen-test engagement targeting the same endpoints
  • Legacy application using PSEMHUB.war for environment metadata sync
Suppression filter
| where ua !has_any ("Qualys","Nessus","Tenable","Rapid7","InsightVM") and src !in ("<your_scanner_subnet>","<your_oracle_support_bastion>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on src IP — confirm whether it's an authorised scanner / partner integration. Pull the full request body from the upstream WAF; presence of `XMLDecoder` or base64-encoded serialized Java markers (`rO0`, `\xac\xed\x00\x05`) confirms exploit attempt. 2) Contain: block source IP at perimeter, apply Oracle's emergency mitigation for CVE-2026-35273 (disable PSEMHUB.war or restrict /PSEMHUB/* to internal /24s only), rotate WebLogic/PeopleSoft service-account credentials on the targeted host. 3) Hunt: on the same host search DeviceFileEvents for new .jsp under PSEMHUB.war (UC3), DeviceProcessEvents for WebLogic Java process spawning hostname/id/grep psappsrv.cfg (UC2), and outbound DNS to azurenetfiles.net (UC4).
// CVE-2026-35273 staging-IP touch on PeopleSoft web tier — Defender can't see HTTP path, so pivot on the published staging /29 hitting PeopleSoft hosts on 80/443.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess")
| where LocalPort in (80,443,8000,8443,7777,7778)   // PeopleTools/WebLogic default listeners
| where RemoteIP in ("142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunts CVE-2026-35273 exploit attempts in IIS / reverse-proxy WAF logs.
let StagingIPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  ( W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where csMethod =~ "POST"
  | where csUriStem has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub","/PSEMHUB/envmetadata","/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, src=cIP, method=csMethod, uri=csUriStem, ua=csUserAgent, status=scStatus, bytes=csBytes ),
  ( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
  | where RequestURL has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub","/PSEMHUB/envmetadata","/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, src=SourceIP, method=RequestMethod, uri=RequestURL, ua=RequestClientApplication, status=tostring(EventOutcome), bytes=ReceivedBytes ))
| extend StagingHit = iff(src in (StagingIPs), "YES", "")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WebLogic/Java spawning Linux recon shell after PSEMHUB exploit AIActions on Objectives High
Post-exploitation recon chain: the PeopleSoft Java/WebLogic process spawns hostname, id, cat /etc/hosts, grep on psappsrv.cfg, or reads WebLogic config.xml. Article corroboration shows this exact sequence runs immediately after CVE-2026-35273 lands. Rationale: Mandiant report quotes the literal recon commands: `hostname; id`, `grep -hE '^[[:space:]]*(Address=|HostName=)' /u01/app/psoft/ps_config_homes/.../psappsrv.cfg`, `cat <WebLogic_HOME>/config.xml`, `mount | grep psoft`. We anchor on Java→child shell relationship plus those literal config file paths — extremely high signal because a normal WebLogic process never reads its own config.xml or shells out to `hostname` and `id`. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1082 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PeopleSoft admin running a manual environment-mapping script during maintenance
  • Custom monitoring agent (Dynatrace, AppDynamics, OEM) that shells out from the WebLogic JVM to read config.xml
  • PSADMIN tooling that reads psappsrv.cfg during application restart
  • DevOps deployment pipeline that grep's HostName= during automated config validation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("dynatrace","AppDynamics","oem_agent","psadmin") and AccountName !in ("psadmin","oem")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent Java process commandline — confirm it's a PeopleSoft WebLogic instance and capture the listening port. Get the user context (typically `psoft` or `oracle`). 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network, snapshot the volume, preserve `/u01/app/psoft/ps_config_homes/.../webserv/.../PSEMHUB.war/` and `.bash_history` (SHA256 2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35 is the published attacker history file). 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents on the same host for new .jsp under PSEMHUB.war (UC3) and outbound to azurenetfiles.net (UC4); pivot back to web tier for the originating POST to /PSEMHUB/hub.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("java","weblogic.Server","startWebLogic.sh") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("java","weblogic.Server")
| where FileName in ("hostname","id","whoami","uname","mount","cat","grep","sh","bash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psappsrv.cfg","ps_config_homes","/u01/app/psoft","WebLogic","config.xml","/etc/hosts","Address=","HostName=")
   or (FileName in ("hostname","id") and InitiatingProcessFileName has "java")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

JSP webshell drop under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war AIInstallation High
Detects creation of new .jsp / .class / .war files under the PeopleSoft web application directory tree — specifically under PSEMHUB.war and its envmetadata/transactions, persistantstorage, scratchpad subdirectories that the ShinyHunters campaign uses for webshell persistence after CVE-2026-35273. Rationale: Mandiant report names the precise persistence path: `<PS_CFG_HOME>/webserv/<domain>/applications/peoplesoft/PSEMHUB.war/` plus the persistantstorage/scratchpad/envmetadata sub-trees and `.xml` XMLDecoder gadgets under envmetadata/data/environment. JSP/class/WAR drops on a PeopleSoft host outside an Oracle patch window are essentially never benign. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Oracle patch / PeopleTools CPU applied via psadmin during a scheduled maintenance window
  • DBA / SI deploying a custom IB connector .jsp via approved change ticket
  • PeopleSoft Update Manager (PUM) image deployment writing new WAR contents
  • Backup/restore operation rehydrating PSEMHUB.war from snapshot
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("psadmin","oracle-installer","pside","pum-deploy") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("psadmin","oracle")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash and quarantine the dropped file, content-inspect for JSP webshell markers (`Runtime.getRuntime().exec`, `ProcessBuilder`, `pageContext.getServletContext`). Check ownership/timestamps vs. last legitimate Oracle CPU deploy. 2) Contain: stop the WebLogic instance, remove the artifact, redeploy PSEMHUB.war from the official Oracle distribution, rotate the WebLogic admin and PeopleSoft application credentials. 3) Hunt: cross-check `.bash_history` on the host against published SHA256 `2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35`, search every other PeopleSoft host in the fleet for matching artifacts (Malaysia and China campuses are in scope per the article), and check egress to azurenetfiles.net (UC4).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/PSEMHUB.war/","/peoplesoft/PSEMHUB","envmetadata/transactions","envmetadata/data/environment","PSEMHUB.war/persistantstorage","PSEMHUB.war/scratchpad")
| where FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".class" or FileName endswith ".war" or (FileName endswith ".xml" and FolderPath has "envmetadata/data/environment")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("oracle-installer","psadmin","pside")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/PSEMHUB.war/","/peoplesoft/PSEMHUB","envmetadata/transactions","envmetadata/data/environment","PSEMHUB.war/persistantstorage","PSEMHUB.war/scratchpad")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("jsp","class","war") or (TargetFileExtension =~ "xml" and TargetFilePath has "envmetadata/data/environment")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MeshCentral Azure-disguised agent + azurenetfiles.net C2 channel AICommand & Control Medium
Detects ShinyHunters' customised MeshCentral agents (filenames meshagent64-azure-ops.exe, meshagent64-v2.exe, meshagent32-azure-ops.exe, Linux meshagent) and the hardcoded C2 over wss://azurenetfiles.net:443/agent.ashx that masquerades as Microsoft Azure NetApp Files. Rationale: Anchors on four ShinyHunters-specific atoms from the Mandiant report: (1) MeshCentral agent filenames customised with `-azure-ops`/`-v2` masquerading suffixes, (2) the four published SHA256 hashes, (3) the C2 domain `azurenetfiles.net` (impersonating Azure NetApp Files), and (4) the `agent.ashx` WebSocket path. None of these are MeshCentral defaults — legitimate MeshAgent installs use `meshagent` or `meshagent.exe` and customer-specific hostnames, not the `-azure-ops` suffix. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1219 T1071.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT support using a legitimate corporate MeshCentral deployment for remote support (would use customer-internal C2 domain, not azurenetfiles.net)
  • Penetration test using MeshCentral as a Cobalt Strike alternative with simulated infrastructure
  • Azure NetApp Files real-domain typo where DNS resolver returns NXDOMAIN — distinguish via wss:443 connection success
  • Security researcher detonating a public IOC sample in a sandboxed lab
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("<your_meshcentral_support_installer>") and RemoteUrl !has "<your_internal_meshcentral_domain>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the MeshCentral agent SHA256 against the four published hashes; if matched it's confirmed ShinyHunters tooling. Capture process tree, parent (likely WebLogic Java or a dropped .sh on Linux). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block azurenetfiles.net at DNS/proxy/firewall, block the staging /29 (142.11.200.184/29), kill the agent process, preserve memory for the agent's encrypted config blob. 3) Hunt: pivot on the DNS resolver logs to find every other host that resolved azurenetfiles.net (likely lateral peers), check for the fanout.sh script on the host (UC5), and look for zstd-compressed exfil archives (UC6).

ShinyHunters fanout.sh SSH credential spray from PeopleSoft host AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the lateral-movement propagation script the campaign drops as `<victim>_fanout.sh`: invocation of `sshpass -p <pass> ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no` from a PeopleSoft application host, used to spray creds across CSPRD/CSPRD02/appserv directories and deploy the defacement marker fleet-wide. Rationale: Mandiant published the script verbatim: `sshpass -p "$password" ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no $user@$host` and the target tree (`$BASE/webserv/CSPRD`, `$BASE/webserv/CSPRD02`, `$BASE/appserv/prcs`). `sshpass` plus `StrictHostKeyChecking=no` on a PeopleSoft host outside an admin's interactive session is a known-bad combo; the `_fanout.sh` filename suffix is a direct campaign IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1110.004 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / SaltStack provisioning that legitimately uses sshpass during initial bootstrap (rare on production PeopleSoft hosts)
  • DBA running a manual multi-host check script with sshpass during an outage
  • DevOps tool deploying PeopleSoft web nodes via SSH from a build server
  • Pen-test or red-team engagement
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("ansible","salt","awx") and InitiatingProcessFileName !has_any ("ansible-playbook","salt-minion","awx-task")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent of the sshpass process — if it's a Java child or a dropped `.sh` under /tmp/, it's exploit-driven, not admin. Capture the destination host list from the commandline iterations. 2) Contain: kill the script and any spawned ssh sessions, rotate every credential the script could have used (PeopleSoft `psoft`/`oracle`/`weblogic` accounts), block the source host from internal SSH at the network layer. 3) Hunt: on every destination host enumerated by the fanout, search for `README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT` (UC7) and new JSP in PSEMHUB.war (UC3); the article notes Malaysia + China campuses — confirm whether the spray reached those segments.
let Window = 10m;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("sshpass","ssh") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("_fanout.sh","StrictHostKeyChecking=no")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sshpass -p","StrictHostKeyChecking=no","webserv/CSPRD","appserv/prcs","_fanout.sh")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","ansible") or ProcessCommandLine has "_fanout.sh"
| summarize FanoutTargets = dcount(ProcessCommandLine),
            Hosts = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 50),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, Window)
| where FanoutTargets >= 5 or Hosts has "_fanout.sh"
| order by LastSeen desc
let Window = 10m;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("/usr/bin/sshpass","/usr/bin/ssh","sshpass","ssh") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("_fanout.sh","StrictHostKeyChecking=no")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sshpass -p","StrictHostKeyChecking=no","webserv/CSPRD","appserv/prcs","_fanout.sh")
| summarize FanoutTargets = dcount(ActingProcessCommandLine),
            Sample = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 50),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, Window)
| where FanoutTargets >= 5 or tostring(Sample) has "_fanout.sh"
| order by LastSeen desc

zstd / pv archive staging of PeopleSoft exfil on application host AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the published ShinyHunters exfil-staging command pattern — `pv -s <size> | zstd -3 -T0 -o exfil.tar.zst` — and any tar/zstd compression of files from /u01/app/psoft or the PeopleSoft web/app server directories. Article describes 40GB of student records, fee payments, passport numbers and campus portal exports staged for the dark-web leak. Rationale: Mandiant cites the exact staging command: `pv -s "$(du -sb exfil | awk '{print $1}')" | zstd -3 -T0 -o exfil.tar.zst`. The combination of `zstd -T0` (multithreaded), the literal `exfil` filename or `.tar.zst` extension, and a working directory under `/u01/app/psoft`/`ps_config_homes`/`PSEMHUB` is essentially unique to this campaign — admins routinely use tar+gzip, not zstd, on PeopleSoft hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA running an authorised export of PeopleSoft data warehouse with tar+zstd compression
  • Backup job using zstd for log archival on the WebLogic host
  • Performance-tuning engineer using `pv` to throttle a known data move
  • Migration project compressing PS_CFG_HOME to ship to a new host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("psadmin","backupops","oracle") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("backup-job","netbackup","rman_export")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the target file path of the archive (-o argument). If the archive resides in /tmp/, /var/tmp/, or a dot-prefixed dir on a PeopleSoft host, treat as confirmed exfil staging. Compute size and compare to article-disclosed 40GB scale. 2) Contain: kill the compression process before completion, preserve any partial .tar.zst as evidence, block egress to azurenetfiles.net and the staging /29, freeze the host's outbound bandwidth at the firewall. 3) Hunt: identify what was read into the archive via auditd PATH records, search for subsequent SFTP/SCP/curl/wget to external destinations, and cross-check against UC4 (MeshCentral C2) for the egress channel.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("zstd","tar","pv","7z","7za","7zz")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("exfil",".tar.zst","/u01/app/psoft","ps_config_homes","PSEMHUB","-T0","webserv/CSPRD")
   or (FileName =~ "zstd" and ProcessCommandLine has "-T0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/usr/bin/zstd","/usr/bin/tar","/usr/bin/pv","/usr/bin/7z","zstd","tar","pv","7z")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("exfil",".tar.zst","/u01/app/psoft","ps_config_homes","PSEMHUB","webserv/CSPRD")
   or (ActingProcessName has "zstd" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-T0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine

ShinyHunters defacement README drop on PeopleSoft hosts AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the campaign's literal extortion marker file `README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT` anywhere on a PeopleSoft host. Per Mandiant the fanout.sh script writes this file to CSPRD/CSPRD02/appserv/prcs directories on every host it reaches. Rationale: Single literal filename `README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT` published by Mandiant as the ShinyHunters defacement marker. Zero realistic false positives — no legitimate process creates this filename. The file appears on every host the fanout.sh script reaches. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1491.001 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Incident-response team placing a copy of the artefact in a quarantine directory during evidence collection
  • Tabletop or purple-team exercise simulating the campaign
  • Security awareness training screenshot directory
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a critical alert — treat as confirmed compromise on the host until proven otherwise. Open an IR ticket, snapshot the host, hash the README and any sibling files in the same folder. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately; if the file appeared on multiple hosts within minutes you're seeing fleet-wide fanout — block all SSH between PeopleSoft hosts at the network layer, force-rotate every shared service account (psoft, oracle, weblogic), and engage Oracle on CVE-2026-35273 emergency mitigation. 3) Hunt: across the entire estate (including Malaysia/China campus segments noted in the article) search for the same filename, JSP webshells under PSEMHUB.war (UC3), MeshCentral binaries / C2 (UC4), and zstd staging archives (UC6). Notify Action Fraud / ICO if data exposure is confirmed.

GitHub to Disable npm Install Scripts by Default to Stop Supply Chain Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has announced what it said are "breaking changes" coming to npm version 12, one of which turns off install scripts by default to combat software supply chain threats. The changes aim to combat attack techniques that abuse the "npm install" command to trigger the execution of malicious code using npm lifecycle hooks. "Npm install" is used to download and install all the necessary

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1528

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Dependency Confusion or Typosquatting Installation · [LLM] npm registry traffic to non-allowlisted registry host during install · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GitHub to Disable npm Install Scripts by Default to Stop Supply Chain Attacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm Post-Install Script Execution from Untrusted Package · [LLM] Suspicious npm Registry Authentication or Publish Activity · [LLM] Lateral Movement via Compromised Transitive Dependency · [LLM] npm pre/post-install Script Disabling Bypass Attempt
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
npm Post-Install Script Execution from Untrusted Package AIInstallation Medium
Detects child processes (PowerShell, cmd, bash, node) spawned by npm/node during install lifecycle hooks (preinstall/install/postinstall) — the exact code-execution surface GitHub is closing in npm 12. Flags developer or CI hosts where lifecycle scripts kick off interpreters, network egress tools, or implicit node-gyp rebuilds (binding.gyp). Rationale: Uses the article's explicit description of preinstall/install/postinstall lifecycle hooks as the npm code-execution surface, plus the named implicit node-gyp rebuild + binding.gyp path. Parent-child predicate is paired with suspicious child + cmdline content so it is not a bare 'powershell.exe' fire. Cross-checked against: • https://github.blog/changelog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/001/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native-module packages (sharp, sqlite3, node-sass, bcrypt) triggering node-gyp rebuild that shells out to cmd.exe
  • Internal devops scripts wrapping `npm install` in a PowerShell installer
  • CI runners (Jenkins, GitHub Actions runner) where npm install spawns bash/sh as the shell
  • Postinstall scripts that legitimately call curl/wget to fetch platform-specific binaries (e.g. Cypress, Puppeteer, Electron)
  • Yarn/pnpm wrappers invoking node.exe which spawns sh.exe on Windows for cross-platform script support
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","sharp","sqlite3","node-sass","bcrypt","puppeteer","cypress","electron") and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","node-gyp.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full process tree (npm.exe → child) and the package.json being installed (CWD of the npm.exe parent). Identify which package's lifecycle script ran (npm logs in %APPDATA%\npm-cache\_logs). 2) Contain — kill the child process, snapshot the host, remove the offending package from node_modules and quarantine the developer/CI cache. If a CI runner, revoke any tokens stored in that runner's environment. 3) Hunt — search org-wide for the same package@version in lockfiles (`package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`), all hosts that ran the install in the last 30 days, and any outbound C2 connections from those hosts. Submit the package SHA to npm security and threat-intel feeds.

   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","npm add","npm i ","node-gyp rebuild","binding.gyp")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","-enc ","-EncodedCommand","http://","https://","FromBase64String","WebClient")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","postinstall","node-gyp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(npm|node|npx|yarn|pnpm)\.exe$/i OR regex("(npm install|npm ci|node-gyp rebuild|binding\.gyp|preinstall|postinstall)", field=ParentCommandLine)
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|bash|sh|wscript|cscript|curl|wget|certutil|bitsadmin|mshta)\.exe$/i
| regex("(DownloadString|Invoke-WebRequest|IEX|-EncodedCommand|FromBase64String|WebClient|https?://)", field=CommandLine)
